nameStory: The "sessileleaf" part of this plant's name comes from its distinctive leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - "sessile" means sitting directly on the stem. The "ticktrefoil" part refers to its three-leaflet leaves (trefoil means three-leaf) and its notorious sticky seed pods that cling to clothing and fur like tiny ticks!
description: Sessileleaf ticktrefoil is a native wildflower that grows as an upright plant, typically reaching 2-4 feet tall. It's part of the legume family, related to beans and peas, and produces small pink to purple pea-like flowers in late summer. The plant has the characteristic three-part leaves of the ticktrefoil family, but unlike most of its relatives, these leaves sit directly on the stem without leaf stalks. After flowering, it develops segmented seed pods that break apart and stick tenaciously to anything that brushes against them.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves that attach directly to the stem with no leaf stalks - run your finger along the stem and you'll feel where the leaf base meets the stem immediately. The leaflets are typically oval-shaped with smooth or slightly toothed edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple pea-like flowers arranged in loose clusters at the stem tips. Each flower is about 1/4 inch long with the typical legume flower shape - one large upper petal and smaller lower petals.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, segmented seed pods that feel slightly fuzzy and break into triangular sections. These sections are covered with tiny hooked hairs that grab onto fabric and fur with surprising tenacity - you'll need to pull them off deliberately.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright, branching plant 2-4 feet tall with a somewhat open, airy appearance. The stems are green to reddish and feel slightly rough to the touch.

habitat: Look for sessileleaf ticktrefoil in dry, open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and partial shade, often growing alongside other native wildflowers in areas that get some sunlight filtering through the canopy. You might find it in old fields that are transitioning back to forest or along woodland trails.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic three-part leaves, making identification possible even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: The plant reaches full size and begins flowering in late summer, typically July through August, when the small pink-purple flowers appear in loose clusters.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods develop and mature, becoming the plant's most noticeable feature as they stick to anyone walking through the area. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and any remaining seed pod segments that haven't been carried away by animals or hikers.

funFact: The hooked hairs on ticktrefoil seed pods are so effective that they inspired part of the design for Velcro - nature created this "hook and loop" fastening system millions of years before humans thought of it!
confusionNotes: With 10 other ticktrefoil species in New England, identification can be tricky, but sessileleaf ticktrefoil's leaves sitting directly on the stem (no leaf stalks) make it unique among its relatives. Memory trick: "sessile" sounds like "sit" - the leaves sit right on the stem!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "ticktrefoil," this plant has nothing to do with disease-carrying ticks - the name refers only to how the seed pods stick like ticks to clothing and fur. As a legume, it actually helps enrich soil by fixing nitrogen through bacteria in its roots.
compareHints: Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems. The showy tick-trefoil has much larger flowers and longer leaf stalks, while panicled ticktrefoil has narrow leaflets and distinct leaf stalks. If you can easily see where the leaf connects to a small stalk before joining the main stem, it's not sessileleaf ticktrefoil.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
